Find a value's index in a sorted array by repeatedly halving the range it could be in.

Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/binary-search) (MIT). Listed under [Collections & Algorithms](/examples/?subject=collections-and-algorithms).

```nomi-run
// FILE: binary_search.nomi
//# Binary search for a value in a sorted vector.

/// The index of `value` in `items`, which must be sorted, found by halving
/// the range it could be in.
pub fn find<T>(items: Vector<T>, value: T) -> Result<Int, String> where T: Comparable {
    search(items, value, 0, Vector.length(items))
}

/// Searches the indices from `low` up to, not including, `high`.
fn search<T>(
    items: Vector<T>,
    value: T,
    low: Int,
    high: Int,
) -> Result<Int, String> where T: Comparable {
    if low >= high { return Err("value not in array") }

    middle = (low + high) / 2
    item = Vector.get(items, middle)!

    case Comparable.compare(value, item) {
        .Less -> search(items, value, low, middle)
        .Equal -> Ok(middle)
        .Greater -> search(items, value, middle + 1, high)
    }
}

// FILE: binary_search_test.nomi
import binary_search

test "finds a value" {
    cases = [
        #("finds a value in an array with one element", #[6], 6, 0),
        #("finds a value in the middle of an array", #[1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11], 6, 3),
        #("finds a value at the beginning of an array", #[1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11], 1, 0),
        #("finds a value at the end of an array", #[1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11], 11, 6),
        #(
            "finds a value in an array of odd length",
            #[1, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55, 89, 144, 233, 377, 634],
            144,
            9,
        ),
        #(
            "finds a value in an array of even length",
            #[1, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55, 89, 144, 233, 377],
            21,
            5,
        ),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, items, value, expected), description {
        assert binary_search.find(items, value) == Ok(expected)
    }
}

test "reports a missing value" {
    cases = [
        #("identifies that a value is not included in the array", #[1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11], 7),
        #(
            "a value smaller than the array's smallest value is not found",
            #[1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11],
            0,
        ),
        #(
            "a value larger than the array's largest value is not found",
            #[1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11],
            13,
        ),
        #("nothing is found in an empty array", #[], 1),
        #("nothing is found when the left and right bounds cross", #[1, 2], 0),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, items, value), description {
        assert binary_search.find(items, value) == Err("value not in array")
    }
}
```

## How it's written

- The input is a `Vector<T>`, not a `List<T>`, since binary search needs indexed access and `List` has none.
- The function is generic over `T: Comparable` and branches on `Comparable.compare` returning `Ordering`, so all three outcomes are one exhaustive `case`.
- A missing value is `Err("value not in array")`, the canonical message. `Maybe<Int>` would have been as natural for "not found".
- Recursion over a half-open range `low..high`; each recursive call is in tail position.
- The middle element is read with `Vector.get(items, middle)!`, which returns the element and traps on an index outside the vector. `middle` is in `low..high` by construction, so there is no miss to handle.
- Two `subtests` tables: found values, and missing values, which assert a different shape.
